newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuela labor strife rolls on, but ministers firm.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela labor strife rolls on, but ministers firm.

text.p: Demonstrating Venezuelan public sector workers linked arms and made a human chain around Congress in a peaceful protest Wednesday for steep pay rises, but government officials stood firm on earlier wage offers.

Some 2,000 public state-employed professionals -- including dentists, teachers, university professors, engineers, and nurses -- waved banners in Caracas's leafy Plaza Bolivar and asked Congress to directly approve a $1,000 minimum wage, so by-passing the executive.

"We'll continue protesting across the whole country," said Elio Mazanero, who represents the Technician's and Professional's Forum, an umbrella group of 29 unions that gathers 500,000 state employees. Radio reports said similar marches simultaneously took place in eastern oil town Maracaibo.
With real wages shrunk by years of inflation to some 30 percent of 1980 levels, the march was the latest in a series of Venezuelan public sector strikes and labor protests.

"The government can't keep on paying us such miserable wages," said Manuel Molina, head of the National College of Journalists, who estimates 90 percent of Venezuelan professionals earn less than 100,000 bolivars ($210) a month. The basic food basket for six costs $250 a month, according to government estimates.
"This wasting-away of our pay is not only encouraging a brain drain from this country," he said, standing next to a banner that read 'We won't give in to the government or the IMF.'
"It's also forcing professionals to abandon their career for the informal economy," he added. According to government statistics, some 50 percent of labor force works in the informal sector.
Increasing calls by public sector workers for wage increases of 100 percent, and more, follow a 164 percent pay rise granted by the government to doctors earlier this year.
To many, that hike has left the government's initial 25 percent public sector wage offer a distant memory.
And many analysts fear escalating claims by Venezuela's 1.3 million public sector workers will bust the budget and send inflation soaring beyond the official 25 percent target for the year.
Planning Minister Teodoro Petkoff said Tuesday each extra 100 billion bolivars ($210 million) spent by the government translated into a 1.5 percent rise in monthly inflation.
"If we grant a large rise to the public sector, everyone else suffers (through inflation)," he said.
But Finance Minister Luis Raul Matos Azocar, speaking in London on Wednesday during an official two day visit, said the doctors' deal did not set a precedent that would pressure the 1997 budget.
"We expect no modifications of the 1.3 billion bolivars (for public sector wage rises) in the budget," he told reporters.
"The medical sector we increased, but we are very firm in our negotiations with the rest of the sector," he added.
